title: Traffic Gradualizer and Safety Handlers for Progressive Delivery
creator: Ava Patel
description: Implement an extensible 'Traffic Gradualizer' service + Safety Handlers to standardize canaries, percentage traffic ramps, flag gate checks, and autonomous rollback triggers across Redwood Inference deployments (hosted, dedicated, private). The goal is to provide a single, auditable control plane for progressive delivery policies that integrates with existing routing, telemetry, and RBAC systems.
rollout_plan: 1) Canary stage: route 0.5% of traffic to new model/service variant for 30m with detailed KPI collection. 2) Ramp stages: 0.5 -> 2 -> 10 -> 30 -> 100 percent with configurable hold windows and health checks at each step. 3) Feature gates: integrate with feature flag service to enable/disable new behaviors per-customer. 4) Auto-rollback: evaluate latency p50/p95, error-rate, and QA synthetic checks; rollback on breach of any critical threshold or repeated regression across 2 consecutive stages.
safety_rules: - Critical thresholds: error-rate increase >2x baseline OR absolute error-rate >0.5% triggers immediate rollback. - Latency: p95 increase >40% over baseline OR p50 increase >60ms triggers pause and notify. - Data-safety: requests flagged as 'sensitive' will not be routed to non-compliant private deployments until manual approval. - Maximum ramp step: no jump >4x previous percentage without explicit approval.
test_plan: Unit tests for policy evaluation, integration tests against local routing shim, e2e with staging cluster using synthetic traffic for 48h, chaos tests that induce node failures during ramps, and canary abort tests that simulate metric regressions. Add test harness to replay historical traffic slices for cost/latency validation.
metrics_and_alerting: Per-stage dashboards (throughput, p50/p95 latency, token cost, error-rate, model-quality regression metrics), automated alerts in PagerDuty for critical breaches, non-critical notifications in Slack dev-channel. Store per-rollout traces for 30 days with links from rollout UI.
decisions: Use a central Gradualizer microservice rather than embedding ramp logic in each router to enforce consistency and easier audit logging.
Represent rollout policy as a small declarative DSL (YAML) that maps to internal gate checks and can be persisted in DB for history and rollback analysis.
Auto-rollback will be conservative (favor availability) and always generate an incident note + rollback justification for postmortem.
Initial rollout cadence will be limited to runtime-hosted and dedicated; private/VPC will have a manual approval checkbox due to compliance constraints.
tradeoffs: Centralized service adds extra hop in routing path (latency impact minimal if cached); tradeoff accepted for consistency and auditability.
Conservative rollback thresholds reduce release velocity but protect customer-facing SLA; plan to iterate thresholds based on observed false-positive rate.
Keeping private deployments manual increases friction for enterprise customers but reduces compliance risk; future roadmap includes an opt-in automated path with stricter guardrails.

review_feedback: PM (Jordan Lee): request to expose per-customer opt-out and explicit billing impact estimates in rollout UI.

risk_assessment: Medium. Primary risks are false positive rollbacks during noisy production windows and edge-case policy evaluation races when multiple rollouts overlap. Mitigations: conservative thresholds, per-rollout cooldown, and serialized policy application for a given model-service pair.
